title: Shapes of molecules
keyIdea: Pairs of electrons round a central atom repel, so they spread out in 3D as far apart as they can. Count the regions: each bond counts once, even a double bond, and each lone pair counts too. Two regions give a linear shape (180°), three give trigonal planar (120°) and four give tetrahedral (109.5°). Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so NH₃ is pyramidal (107°) and H₂O is bent (104.5°).

kid: Electrons come in pairs round the central atom of a molecule. Pairs repel each other, so they spread out as far as they can. They spread in 3D, not just flat on the page. That is why methane, CH₄, is not a flat cross.

Count the regions of electrons round the central atom. Each bond is one region, and so is each double bond. Two regions sit 180° apart, as in CO₂: a linear shape. Three spread to 120°, as in BF₃: trigonal planar.

Four regions point to the corners of a tetrahedron. The bond angle is 109.5°, as in CH₄. A lone pair is a pair of electrons that is not in a bond. It still takes up a region, but we name the shape from the atoms we can see.

Lone pairs push harder than bonds, so they squeeze the bonds closer. NH₃ has 3 bonds and 1 lone pair: it is pyramidal, at 107°. H₂O has 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs: it is bent, at 104.5°. Each lone pair takes about 2.5° off.
adult: This A-level chemistry topic (ages 16 to 18) uses valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) theory. The shape of a simple molecule or ion follows from the number of electron-pair regions round the central atom: bonding pairs and lone pairs, with a double or triple bond counted as one region.

Learners should know linear (2 regions, 180°), trigonal planar (3, 120°), tetrahedral (4, 109.5°), pyramidal (3 bonding + 1 lone pair, about 107°) and bent (2 bonding + 2 lone pairs, about 104.5°). The order of repulsion is lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair, because a lone pair is held by one nucleus and sits closer to it.

Common mistakes: reading the flat drawing of CH₄ as 90°; counting a double bond as two regions; leaving lone pairs out, so NH₃ is called trigonal planar and H₂O linear; naming the shape from the regions rather than the atoms; giving 109.5° for NH₃ and H₂O; and counting lone electrons instead of pairs.

In the lab, learners squeeze a bond and watch it spring back, turn the molecule in 3D, build linear and trigonal planar shapes, add a lone pair to make NH₃, compare CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O, and work out PH₃ and H₂S from outer electrons. The challenge asks for the shape and angle of six species, including CO₂ and NH₄⁺.

familyTip: Tie four balloons together at their knots. They push apart into a tetrahedron by themselves, just like the electron pairs in methane. Try two and three balloons to see the linear and flat triangle shapes.

practice.prompt: What is the shape of a molecule with 4 bonding pairs and no lone pairs round the central atom?
practice.hint: Four pairs spread out as far as they can in 3D.
practice.explain: Four regions point to the corners of a tetrahedron, 109.5° apart, as in CH₄. A flat square would put them only 90° apart.

practice.prompt: A central atom has {a} bonding pairs and {b} lone pairs. How many regions of electrons are round it?
practice.hint: Bonding pairs and lone pairs both count as regions.
practice.explain: Regions = {a} bonding + {b} lone = {=a+b}. Lone pairs take up space just like bonds do, so both are counted.

practice.prompt: Why is the bond angle in NH₃ (107°) smaller than in CH₄ (109.5°)?
choices: The lone pair repels more strongly than a bonding pair
N is a smaller atom than C
NH₃ has fewer electrons in total
practice.hint: What does N have that C in CH₄ does not?
practice.explain: N has a lone pair. It repels more than a bonding pair, so it pushes the three N–H bonds a little closer together.

practice.prompt: A central atom has {a} outer electrons and makes {b} single bonds to H atoms. How many lone pairs does it have?
practice.hint: Each bond to H uses one of its outer electrons. Pair up the rest.
practice.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b} electrons are left over. Pair them up: {=(a-b)/2} lone pairs.

practice.prompt: How many regions of electrons are round the C atom in CO₂ (O=C=O)?
practice.hint: A double bond points one way. Does it count once or twice?
practice.explain: Each double bond is one region, so C has 2 regions. They sit 180° apart and CO₂ is linear.

pool.prompt: What is the shape of a water molecule, H₂O?
pool.hint: O has 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs. Name the shape from the atoms.
pool.explain: The 4 regions are roughly tetrahedral, but only 2 hold atoms, so the shape is bent. The 2 lone pairs squeeze the angle to 104.5°.

pool.prompt: BF₃ has 3 bonding pairs and no lone pairs on B. What shape is it?
pool.hint: Three regions with no lone pair spread out in one plane.
pool.explain: Three regions get furthest apart at 120° in a flat triangle. There is no lone pair to push them into a pyramid.

pool.prompt: Put these repulsions in order, strongest first.
pool.hint: Lone pairs sit closer to the central atom and spread wider.
pool.explain: Lone pairs repel most, so lone–lone is strongest and bond–bond is weakest. That is why each lone pair closes the bond angle.

pool.prompt: Sam says NH₃ is trigonal planar because N has three bonds. What did he miss?
choices: The lone pair on N, which makes 4 regions
pool.hint: N has 5 outer electrons. How many are used in bonds?
pool.explain: N uses 3 electrons in bonds and keeps 2 as a lone pair. With 4 regions the shape is pyramidal, not flat.

pool.prompt: What is the shape of the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺?
pool.hint: The lone pair of NH₃ is used to bond the fourth H⁺.
pool.explain: NH₄⁺ has 4 bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so it is tetrahedral at 109.5°, like CH₄.

pool.prompt: A central atom has {a} regions of electrons, and {b} of them are lone pairs. How many bonding pairs does it have?
pool.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b} bonding pairs. The lone pairs still count as regions, but they hold no atoms.

pool.prompt: Why is CH₄ not a flat cross with 90° angles?
choices: In 3D the pairs can get further apart, at 109.5°
The H atoms attract each other
pool.hint: Electron pairs spread as far apart as they can. Are they stuck on the page?
pool.explain: A flat cross only gives 90°. Spreading in 3D to the corners of a tetrahedron gives 109.5°, which is further apart.

pool.prompt: A central atom has {b} outer electrons and makes {a} single bonds to H atoms. How many regions of electrons are round it?
pool.hint: Each bond is one region. Pair up the electrons not used in bonds to find the lone pairs.
pool.explain: {a} bonds + {=(b-a)/2} lone pairs = {=a+(b-a)/2} regions of electrons round the central atom.

visual.caption: Which shape? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: squeeze and turn a 3D molecule, add bonds and lone pairs to build each shape, and watch lone pairs close the bond angle.
